191: Total antioxidant activity (Table 4.15 and Fig. 4.15) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (426.88 mg TE 100 g⁻¹), followed by GBI (389.72 mg TE 100 g⁻¹), and lowest in DI (165.26 mg TE 100 g⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 393.45 in the beet fortified product, 287.71 in the carrot fortified product and 185.29 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (314.45) and lowest in Dudeshwar (265.88).
192: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 1.13, with a coefficient of variation of 0.34 per cent.
194: The most probable basis of the antioxidant activity pattern is that the antioxidant capacity of a cereal-based food is governed almost entirely by its phenolic and flavonoid pool, so that this character necessarily followed those two fractions. The relationship is well established for rice and for whole grains generally (Adom and Liu, 2002; Liu, 2007; Shao et al., 2014; Goufo and Trindade, 2014) and is confirmed in the present study by the very high correlations recorded between the three fractions. The betalains of beetroot make an additional and independent contribution, being powerful hydrogen donors with a radical-scavenging capacity comparable with that of the common flavonoids (Kanner et al., 2001; Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Ravichandran et al., 2013). Fermentation may raise the measured activity further by liberating bound phenolics into the free and more readily assayed form, an increase reported in fermented rice, barley and oat products (Dordevic et al., 2010; Hole et al., 2012; Ti et al., 2014). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) likewise reported that the insoluble bound fraction of idli carried the highest antioxidant activity of the three phenolic fractions, which confirms the bound phenolics of the bran layer to be the principal contributors to the antioxidant capacity of the product.
203: Beta-carotene content (Table 4.16 and Fig. 4.16) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KCI (45.77), followed by GCI (43.59), and lowest in DI (0.00). Among the products the mean value was 38.85 in the carrot fortified product, 2.44 in the beet fortified product and 0.00 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (15.93) and lowest in Dudeshwar (10.92).
204: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.08, with a coefficient of variation of 0.48 per cent.
206: Carrot constituted the only meaningful source of provitamin A in this study, which is the evident and most probable basis of the pattern recorded. Carrot ranks among the richest dietary sources of all-trans beta-carotene, and its carotenoids are located in chromoplasts readily ruptured during grinding, so that the pigment is efficiently transferred to the batter (Britton, 1995; Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). Milled rice and black gram carry essentially no carotenoid, which accounts for the nil values of the plain treatments (Champagne, 2004; Gopalan et al., 2004). The good retention of the pigment in the finished product is attributable to the mild processing conditions, all-trans beta-carotene being reasonably stable under the brief moist heat of steaming but rapidly lost under frying or prolonged dry heating (Delgado-Vargas et al., 2000; Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001). The mildly acidic pH generated by fermentation may additionally afford some protection against isomerisation and oxidation during the batter stage (Blandino et al., 2003).
215: Anthocyanin content (Table 4.17 and Fig. 4.17) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (1.86), followed by RBI (1.53), and lowest in DCI (0.00). Among the products the mean value was 1.41 in the beet fortified product, 0.00 in the plain product and 0.00 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (0.62) and lowest in Dudeshwar (0.33).
216: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.06, with a coefficient of variation of 9.63 per cent.
218: The most probable basis of the anthocyanin pattern is that the pigment derived from two sources, both present only in certain treatments. The principal source was the betacyanin fraction of beetroot, which is determined together with anthocyanin by the spectrophotometric method employed and which was introduced only into the beet fortified treatments (Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Azeredo, 2009; Chhikara et al., 2019). The second and smaller source was the pigment carried over from the black-husked kernel of Kalojira, which accounts for this variety recording the highest value within the beet fortified group (Sompong et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2014). The retention of the pigment in the finished product is attributable to the mildly acidic pH generated during lactic fermentation, betalains and anthocyanins alike being most stable in the pH range of approximately four to six and degrading rapidly under alkaline conditions or prolonged heating (Herbach et al., 2006; Azeredo, 2009; Ravichandran et al., 2013).
229: Copper content (Table 4.18 and Fig. 4.18) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in GBI (0.97 mg L⁻¹), followed by DCI (0.78 mg L⁻¹), and lowest in DI (0.21 mg L⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 0.48 in the beet fortified product, 0.46 in the carrot fortified product and 0.26 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (0.56) and lowest in Kalojira (0.28).
230: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 9.65 per cent.
232: Copper is largely a varietal character determined by the mineral status of the parent grain and by the soil on which it was grown, which constitutes the most probable basis of the clear separation of the varieties recorded here (Rani et al., 2006; Hemalatha et al., 2007; Gopalan et al., 2004). Gobindabhog carried the best overall mineral profile of the four varieties, consistent with its highest ash content. The rise on fortification is attributable to the copper contributed by the vegetable extract itself, beetroot constituting a modest but useful source of trace elements (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). The availability of copper, like that of the other divalent cations, is contingent upon the phytate content of the product, and the reduction of phytate during soaking and fermentation is likely to have improved its accessibility (Sandberg, 2002; Lestienne et al., 2005; Hotz and Gibson, 2007).
241: Iron content (Table 4.19 and Fig. 4.19) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in RI (3.36 mg L⁻¹), followed by GI (2.99 mg L⁻¹), and lowest in DI (1.36 mg L⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 2.30 in the plain product, 1.77 in the beet fortified product and 1.73 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (2.51) and lowest in Kalojira (1.52).
242: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 1.77 per cent.
244: The most probable basis of iron being highest in the plain products of the aromatic landraces is that the grain itself constitutes the principal source of this element, so that any addition of a low-iron vegetable extract dilutes it (Rani et al., 2006; Gopalan et al., 2004; Chhikara et al., 2019). The varietal differences recorded reflect genuine differences in grain iron between the landraces, a variation well documented in rice germplasm (Champagne, 2004; Hemalatha et al., 2007). Although rice-based diets are generally poor in available iron, the soaking and fermentation steps preceding steaming improve its accessibility considerably by activating phytase and lowering the phytate to iron molar ratio, an improvement demonstrated for rice, wheat and legume systems alike (Sandberg, 2002; Lestienne et al., 2005; Hotz and Gibson, 2007; Liang et al., 2008). The practical value of the present result therefore resides as much in the processing method as in the absolute iron content.
253: Zinc content (Table 4.20 and Fig. 4.20) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in RI (0.89 mg L⁻¹), followed by KBI (0.87 mg L⁻¹), and lowest in DI (0.64 mg L⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 0.76 in the beet fortified product, 0.75 in the plain product and 0.71 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Radhunipagal (0.82) and lowest in Dudeshwar (0.66).
254: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 4.63 per cent.
256: Zinc altered comparatively little with fortification, the probable basis being that the grain and the black gram, rather than the vegetable extract, constitute its principal source in this product (Gopalan et al., 2004; Hemalatha et al., 2007). The differences recorded were therefore chiefly varietal and reflect the grain zinc status of the four landraces (Champagne, 2004; Rani et al., 2006). More consequential than the absolute content is the availability of the zinc present, since phytate binds zinc strongly and a phytate to zinc molar ratio exceeding fifteen is generally taken to indicate poor absorption (Sandberg, 2002; Hemalatha et al., 2007). The soaking and overnight fermentation of the batter activate endogenous and microbial phytase and lower this ratio appreciably, which has been shown to improve zinc solubility in brown rice and in other cereals (Lestienne et al., 2005; Hotz and Gibson, 2007; Liang et al., 2008; Gupta et al., 2015).
265: Manganese content (Table 4.21 and Fig. 4.21) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in GI (0.69 mg L⁻¹), followed by GBI (0.68 mg L⁻¹), and lowest in DI (0.37 mg L⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 0.55 in the beet fortified product, 0.53 in the plain product and 0.53 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (0.64) and lowest in Dudeshwar (0.40).
266: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.72, with a coefficient of variation of 6.91 per cent.
268: Manganese was the only character in the study for which the main effect of fortification proved non-significant, the most probable basis being that neither beetroot nor carrot is a rich source of this element, so that the vegetable extract neither augmented nor appreciably diluted it (Sharma et al., 2012; Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). The differences recorded were therefore essentially varietal and reflect the grain manganese status of the landraces, which is known to vary with genotype and with the soil on which the crop is grown (Rani et al., 2006; Hemalatha et al., 2007; Gopalan et al., 2004). The interaction was nevertheless significant, which indicates that the small response to the extract was not identical in every variety, most probably because the base manganese content differed and because phytate, which likewise binds manganese, differed between the varieties (Sandberg, 2002; Lestienne et al., 2005).
277: Calcium content (Table 4.22 and Fig. 4.22) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in GBI (550.88 mg L⁻¹), followed by DBI (510.62 mg L⁻¹), and lowest in KI (61.44 mg L⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 500.89 in the beet fortified product, 263.31 in the carrot fortified product and 85.07 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (371.86) and lowest in Kalojira (211.38).
278: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.66, with a coefficient of variation of 0.20 per cent.
280: The very large rise in calcium on fortification has an evident and direct cause, namely that beetroot is a good source of calcium and its extract introduces a substantial quantity of the element into the batter (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). Carrot contributes a smaller amount, which accounts for the intermediate position of the carrot fortified treatments (Sharma et al., 2012). Milled rice is very poor in calcium and black gram supplies only a moderate quantity, so that the plain treatments returned the lowest values (Rani et al., 2006; Gopalan et al., 2004). The gain is of practical nutritional importance, since rice-based diets are widely recognised to be deficient in calcium (Gopalan et al., 2004; Oghbaei and Prakash, 2016). It must, however, be read alongside the parallel rise in phytate recorded in the same treatments, since phytate binds calcium and reduces its absorption, so that the phytate to calcium ratio determines what proportion of the added calcium is actually available (Reddy et al., 1982; Sandberg, 2002; Hemalatha et al., 2007).
